pages.text: It rained for five days. Not the brief afternoon rain that arrived and was over before dinner, but a sustained, democratic rain that covered the whole sky from the first hour of morning until dark, sometimes heavier, sometimes lighter, but never completely absent. The estate was damp and quiet. The estate children were mostly indoors.

image.note: Illustration: rain falling on the empty estate road, windows lit in all the buildings

pages.text: On the third day, Emeka went down to the basement block to retrieve something from the family storage cage. He noticed, for the first time, a door at the far end of the corridor that was different from the storage cage doors. It was solid, not grilled. It had a padlock that was old enough to have gone slightly orange at the hinges. And it had a piece of paper taped to it so old that the tape had turned yellow and the paper was soft.
The paper said: Do Not Open Without Management Authorisation. The signature at the bottom was illegible. The date written underneath was 2004.
Emeka looked at the door for a while. Then he went upstairs to find the others.

They were in Chinasa's flat because Chinasa's flat had the best snacks during rain situations. Emeka explained what he had found. There was a brief silence of the kind that means everyone is thinking rather than nobody.

image.note: Illustration: five children in a flat living room, rain visible through the window, all leaning forward in discussion

pages.text: 'Records,' Isa said. 'Management always puts old records in locked rooms. Accounts, correspondence, contracts.' 'They wouldn't lock records with a padlock like that,' Nosa said. 'That kind of padlock is for something you genuinely want to protect. Records go in filing cabinets.' 'Old equipment,' Hanan said. 'Electrical equipment they retired. Estate tools.' 'Old equipment from 2004 is not that interesting,' Chinasa said.

'Maybe it's not from 2004,' Nosa said. 'The sign is from 2004. The door might be older. The padlock is definitely older.' Everyone agreed the padlock was older. 'Then the question,' Emeka said, 'is who put the sign on the door, and who locked it, and whether those were the same person or two different events.'

Chinasa had the most energetic theory, which involved a previous estate manager who had left in a hurry and taken the key but not told anyone why. Ini said this was possible but required more assumption than the evidence supported. Chinasa said assumptions were not always wrong. Ini agreed they were not always wrong. They did not agree further.

The rain settled over the estate like a decision that had been made and would not be unmade. It filled the gutters and overflowed them, turned the car park into a sheet of moving water, and drove every child indoors to invent the particular kinds of games that only get invented on the third day of rain. It was during one of these, a hunt for something in the basement storage, that Emeka found the door, and once he had found it he could not stop thinking about it.

A locked door is one thing. A locked door with a sign so old the tape had gone brown, a padlock rusted at the hinges, and a date twenty years past, is another thing entirely. It was a small mystery, and small mysteries, on the third day of rain, grow quickly to fill the space available. By the time Emeka reached Chinasa's flat, where the best snacks and the best arguments were both reliably found, the door had grown in his mind into something that had to be opened.

The others took it up at once, because there was nothing else to do and because a sealed room is irresistible to anyone under the age of about ninety. Isa wanted to know who had signed the sign. Nosa wanted to know why a padlock so serious guarded a room nobody remembered. Chinasa wanted, frankly, for it to contain treasure, and said so, and was not embarrassed. Ini said nothing yet, but Ini was thinking, and when Ini was thinking it usually meant the answer was closer than anyone else believed.

Mr Obi had the key. This was established after a conversation with his assistant, who checked a key registry that went back eleven years, at the end of which she discovered a key logged as 'basement store original' that had never been signed out.

image.note: Illustration: Mr Obi's assistant at a desk with a large key registry book, a key on a ring on the page

pages.text: Mr Obi agreed to open the room on the basis that, twenty years after the lock had last been touched, the contents should probably be inventoried regardless of what they were. He brought a torch. The padlock opened after some persuasion and a small amount of oil that Vitalis provided from his maintenance kit.
The room was dry, which was the first surprising thing. The building sealed it effectively enough to keep the moisture out. The second surprising thing was what was inside.

Mosaic panels. Twelve of them, wrapped in cloth and stacked carefully against the wall. Not crammed. Not discarded. Placed with care, as though the person who put them there expected to come back for them. Each panel was approximately one metre square. Each depicted something from Nigerian life: a market scene, a fishing boat, a savannah sunset, an eagle in flight.

image.note: Illustration: the unwrapped mosaic panels leaning against the wall, colourful and detailed, Mr Obi and children looking at them in torchlight

pages.text: Mr Obi called the estate's founding documents from the company archive. It took two days. The documents confirmed that the mosaics had been commissioned in 1987 as part of the original estate fit-out, installed in the lobby and main corridors, and removed in 2004 during a refurbishment that replaced them with the current pale tiles. The removal order said they were to be stored temporarily pending a decision about relocation. The decision had never been made. The company had changed ownership in 2011 and the archive had not been fully reviewed since. Nobody who had been involved in the 2004 decision still worked there.

'They have been here for twenty years,' Emeka said. He was looking at the fishing boat panel, which was missing one small tile from the top right corner but was otherwise intact. 'Twenty-one,' Mr Obi said. He also appeared to be looking at the panels rather than at the paperwork in his hand.

The children proposed, via a letter Emeka drafted, that the panels be restored and reinstalled in the basement corridor and the lobby entrance. The regional director agreed faster than anyone had expected. The restoration took six weeks. The tiles were cleaned and the missing tile in the fishing boat panel was matched and replaced by a specialist.

The rain had long since stopped. On the day the last panel was reinstalled, Chinasa stood in the lobby for a while looking at the market scene. 'They are better than the tiles,' she said. 'Everything is better than the tiles,' Nosa said. Chinasa looked at him. 'You are correct,' she said.

It was not treasure, unless you counted it as treasure, which Chinasa immediately decided she did. It was the estate's own memory, wrapped in cloth and stacked with a care that told its own story: someone, twenty years ago, had put these mosaic panels here meaning to come back for them, and had never come. The market scene. The fishing boat with its one missing tile. The savannah sunset. They had been made for this estate, torn out of it, and forgotten in the dark beneath it.

Mr Obi stood among the panels for a long time without saying anything, which was unlike him, and when he finally spoke it was only to correct himself on the number of years. But the children understood what the silence had been. He was seeing the estate he had managed for a lifetime as it had looked before the pale tiles, before he had arrived, when someone had cared enough to set beauty into its walls. Some things are lost by accident, simply because no one decides to keep them. And some of those things, if you are lucky and it rains for five days, can be found again.
